raw_summary: <cite index="4-1,4-2">Competitors emphasize how equine chiropractic improves mobility, relieves joint restrictions, enhances performance, and supports overall comfort, with horse owners choosing chiropractic care to help their horses move better and recover faster.</cite> <cite index="31-5,31-6">Barrel racing is positioned as one of the most explosive and demanding events, requiring precision, power, speed, and tight turns, with the horse's body needing to function optimally to shave off crucial tenths of a second.</cite> <cite index="30-1,30-6,30-7">Rodeo-focused practitioners like Dr. Cowboy (Justin Beasley) use veterinary orthopedic manipulation (VOM)—a specialized technique similar to chiropractic but more effective in correcting misalignments of vertebrae in bulls and livestock.</cite> <cite index="39-1,39-3">Montana bodywork providers serve ranch horses to rodeo athletes, using massage therapy, myofascial release, and other modalities to relieve tension, prevent injuries, and enhance overall well-being.</cite> <cite index="4-5,4-6">Common presenting issues include gait abnormalities, stiffness, behavioral issues, decreased performance, neck or back pain, and post-injury recovery, with signs including resistance under saddle, uneven stride, trouble bending, difficulty picking up leads, sensitivity to touch, or behavioral changes.</cite> <cite index="42-12,42-17,42-18,42-19">Texas Hill Country practitioners using the Masterson Method emphasize that their approach identifies and releases accumulated tension from the equine body, recognizing and using the horse's responses to touch to find and release tension in key junctions, and when tension is released the horse's performance is improved.</cite> <cite index="26-11,26-12">Performance horses during peak season typically receive spinal manipulations every 4 to 8 weeks, while other horses with more sedentary lifestyles benefit from care every 6 to 12 months.</cite>
